set.st: James H. Webster, an Indiana man who went to the California gold rush in 1852, settled on a farm near Steamboat Rock in 1876. In May 1897 the Steamboat Rock Echo reported that he distrusted banks, had buried about $1,000 of pension money and several hundred dollars more, and then forgot the spot; searching failed. Wire copies that spring inflated it to $50,000 in casks. He was judged insane that spring and died in the state hospital at Independence in August 1897, leaving several thousand dollars of property. A dowser wrote to the probate judge offering to find his money. No dig find was reported. An Eldora dispatch of 5 June 1897 reported that Webster, by then insane, was taken to jail and that four tin cans holding about $2,000 in gold were found on him, which would cover the local paper's estimate of what he had buried. On 24 June 1897 the Echo reported that Webster had been declared insane and that his money and goods, about $3,500, had passed to a court-appointed guardian, with a court order holding his deposit at the Hardin County Bank; the same page carried a Missouri man's letter offering to find the buried money. The estate went intestate in Aug 1897 on a $6,000 bond, which points to about $3,000 of personal property expected, not $50,000.
set.t: The local amount (about $1,000-1,500) is the believable one, and the 1897 record accounts for it: $2,000 in gold found on him, about $3,500 passed to his guardian and bank. One local source (the editor 'can not vouch'); his obituary adds that he was said to carry considerable money on his person, which may mean some of it was never buried. Place Webster's farm in Clay Township on an 1890s Hardin plat. Access: private: permission.
set.tovw: Lead grade F: the $2,000 in gold found on him and the $3,500 that passed to his guardian and the Hardin County Bank account for the believable local sum; the $50,000-in-casks figure was a wire exaggeration
